newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos denies stacking government with military.
newsitem.headline: Ramos denies stacking government with military.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Tuesday dismissed fears his appointment of another former army general to his cabinet was a sign of growing military power in the government.

Opposition politicians had warned that the appointment of retired armed forces chief Arturo Enrile as transportation and communications secretary could lead to dictatorship, allowing Ramos to stay on in office when his six-year term ends next year.
"We expected this kind of criticism," Ramos, himself a former army general, told reporters in northern Nueva Ecija province.

He said the former military and police officers he had appointed to senior government positions -- now totalling more than 40, including five cabinet ministers -- would stay in office only for as long his own presidential term.
"Our graduation day is June 30, 1998," Ramos added, referring to the date when his term as president will end.

In addition to his cabinet appointment, Enrile on Tuesday was elected one of 11 government representatives on the 15-member board of food and beverage giant San Miguel Corp, one of the country's most prominent companies.

A government list shows 29 former military and police generals now hold government posts. They include the secretary of public works, the interior secretary and the presidential adviser on national security.

Other former military men are in charge of a state-run television station, a state gaming corporation, the irrigation office, Manila's international airport, the national railways, the ports, the maritime industry and a state lottery.
"With such a government composition, a dictatorship cannot be far behind if the attempt to amend the constitution is not realised," opposition congressman Joker Arroyo told reporters.
Enrile's appointment "confirms our worst fears about the militarisation of the bureaucracy," Senate defence committee chairman Orlando Mercado said.

The constitution limits a president to one term. Despite Ramos's avowals that he will step down next year, opposition groups have accused him of instigating moves to call a plebiscite to amend the charter so he can run for a second term.
